I would be eight people, and then the difficulties vanish.
Only as one do I contain the complications,
in a warm house roofed with the rib-cage of an elephant.

I pass my grey mornings re-running the reels,
and the images are the same, but the emphasis shifts.
The actors bow gently to me, and I envy them
their repeated parts, their constant presence in that world.

I would be eight people, each inhabiting the others' dreams,
walking through corridors of glass-framed pages,
telling each other the final lines of letters,
picking fruit in one dream and storing it in another.

Only as one do I contain the complications,
and the images are the same—their constant presence in that world.
The actors bow gently to me and envy my grey mornings.

I would be eight people, with the rib-cage of an elephant,
picking fruit in a warm house above actors bowing,
re-running the reels of my presence in this world.

The difficulties vanish, and the images are the same:
eight people, glass corridors, page lines repeated,
inhabiting grey mornings roofed with my complications,
only as one, walking gently, storing my dream.

# On Wishing to Be Many

Sometimes I imagine that I could be eight separate people, and I convince myself that if only this were true, all of life's difficulties would simply dissolve. The burdens I carry would be divided, shared out among these other versions of myself, until each fragment was light enough to bear. In that fantasy, nothing weighs too heavily, because nothing must be held by one person alone.

But this is the trouble with existing as a single, unified self: there is no one to share the weight with. Every complication, every sorrow, every knot of feeling must be contained within one body and endured by one mind. I am the only vessel available, and so everything pours into me and stays there, with nowhere else to go.

I spend my grey mornings replaying memories, running them like old film reels through the projector of my mind. What strikes me is that the images themselves never change—the same faces, the same rooms, the same gestures, frozen exactly as they were. And yet each time I watch them, their emphasis shifts. What once seemed central fades to the background; what I overlooked before suddenly demands my attention. The pictures remain constant, but their meaning refuses to hold still.

And so I find myself envying the actors who appear in these memories, the ones who seem to bow to me from within the screen. They have it easier, I think. They perform their roles again and again, night after night, and they never have to leave. They are permanent, unchanging, fixed forever in that imagined world. I long for that kind of steadiness—that endless, repeated existence that never has to move forward or let go.

In the fullest version of my fantasy, the eight of us would not merely exist side by side; we would be woven together. We would inhabit one another's dreams, passing between them as easily as walking from room to room. In one dream I might pick fruit from a tree, and in another I might store it away—each self reaching into the world of the others, connected by strange and surreal acts that only such a multiplicity could allow. To be eight people, then, is not only to divide the weight, but to belong to something larger than a single life: a web of selves, dreaming into each other, never truly alone.
outputs.L4:
# On Being Eight People

The poem opens with an impossible wish, one that becomes the engine driving everything that follows: the speaker longs to be "eight people." This is not merely a desire for company but something more radical—a yearning to escape the confinement of singular selfhood, to distribute consciousness across multiple bodies, multiple minds, multiple simultaneous lives. To be one, the poem suggests, is a kind of trap, and the speaker dreams of unfolding into plurality the way a single note might blossom into a chord.

At the heart of this longing sits a strange and vivid image: a house built from an elephant's rib-cage. The curved bones form the architecture of a dwelling, and within its shadowed interior the speaker imagines eight sleepers inhabiting shared dreams. There is something both tender and grotesque in this vision—the shelter constructed from the remains of a massive creature, the ribs that once protected a living heart now arching over the small human bodies that sleep beneath them. The image insists on being read as both refuge and remnant, a home made of loss.

The poem does not progress in a straight line. Instead, it moves through cyclical repetition, returning again and again to the same phrases, the same images, but shuffled into new arrangements each time. "Eight people." "Only as one." The rib-cage. The shared dream. Each recurrence lands differently because its neighbors have changed, so that meaning accumulates and shifts like light moving across the same room throughout a day. This recursive structure is not decoration; it is the poem's argument. The circling itself enacts the very fragmentation it describes, the mind turning over the same material, unable to resolve it, unable to move on.

Against the fantasy of multiplicity, the poem sets the hard fact of solitude: to exist "only as one." Loneliness here is not simple emptiness. Rather, singular consciousness is shown to be overcrowded with its own complications—the single self must contain all its contradictions, all its memories, all its unmet needs, with no one to share the burden. Paradoxically, being one is more complicated than being eight, because the eight might divide the weight among themselves, while the one must carry everything alone.

It is against this backdrop that the speaker's envy of actors becomes meaningful. Actors possess what the solitary self cannot: a constant presence and the comfort of repeated roles. Night after night they return to the same stage, speak the same lines, become the same people, and in that repetition they find a kind of stability the speaker cannot access. The actor is many selves by profession, slipping into other lives and returning safely to the wings. The speaker envies this permission to multiply, this sanctioned escape from the prison of the single identity, and envies too the reassurance of knowing that the performance will come again tomorrow, unchanged.

Ultimately, the poem is a meditation on memory and self-division. The recurring images function like memories themselves—returning unbidden, slightly altered, never quite the same twice. The wish to be eight people is finally revealed as the wish not to be so alone inside one's own mind, not to bear the full weight of a single consciousness with all its isolation. The elephant's rib-cage stands as the poem's central emblem: a home made from a body, a shelter that is also a grave, a space large enough to hold many dreamers and yet built entirely from the bones of something now gone. In its restless circling and its impossible arithmetic, the poem gives voice to the deep and universal loneliness of being, irreducibly and inescapably, only one.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental poem in the style of a fragmented dream, using recurring images like an elephant's rib-cage, glass corridors, and actors bowing.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rehearsal for a Vanishing

*

An elephant's rib-cage, but open—
the bars of it letting weather through,
and I walk the inside like a nave
where something enormous used to kneel.

*

Glass corridors. Again the glass.
I press my palm and the whole hall
tilts its long throat of light
and swallows the direction I came from.

*

The actors bow.
They bow before the play.
They bow with their faces still wet
from a scene I was not permitted to see.

*

Someone hands me a program
printed on the inside of an eyelid.
The cast list is only my name,
misspelled, and set in a language of rain.

*

Back in the rib-cage now—
how did I—the bars have grown
into the glass, the glass into
the smell of a curtain that never opens.

*

I am late. I am always the understudy
to my own arrival.
The elephant breathes once,
enormous, and the corridors exhale their doors.

*

The actors bow again, lower,
until their foreheads touch the boards,
until they are not bowing but
lying down inside the great white cage of the animal—

*

and the applause is only
weather, letting itself through.

*

I wake holding a shard
that shows no face,
only the long grey curve
of something that was breathing when I left.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Fractured Chorus

I am one and the many, standing at the window
where the light divides itself into strangers.
Each pane holds a face I recognize but cannot name.
Loneliness is a room with too many mirrors—
I speak, and the echo answers in another's voice.

The self unspools like thread through empty hours.
I am the one who leaves, and the one who stays behind.
Somewhere a version of me is laughing.
Somewhere a version of me forgets my name.

The light divides itself into strangers—
I speak, and the echo answers.
Each pane, each face, unspooling through empty hours,
I am the one who stays, the one who forgets.

Standing at the window, one and the many,
loneliness is a room. I recognize but cannot name
the version laughing, the version leaving,
the thread, the light, the strangers I call *self*.

I speak—
the echo answers in the window's many faces,
where the one who stays
forgets
the one who leaves
is
laughing
is
a stranger
is
me.

Each pane a room. Each face a thread.
The light, the many, the one—
unspooling, unspooling,
answers in another's voice:

*I am. I am. I am the*

stranger
at the window
speaking
to the light
that will not
name me
back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about someone who imagines dividing into multiple selves to escape difficulties, using imagery of houses, dreams, letters, and reels of film.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Multiplication

When the trouble came, I built a house
inside my chest and moved the frightened one there,
gave her a window facing the wrong direction
so she wouldn't have to watch.

Another self I sent into a dream
that keeps repeating—the staircase, the open door—
and left her wandering its patient halls
where nothing is required, only walking.

To a third I gave the task of letters,
the endless correspondence with the world:
*Dear everyone, I'm fine. I'm fine.*
Her hand does not shake as she signs my name.

The rest I wound onto reels of film,
each frame a version who could not stay—
the one who laughed, the one who answered kindly,
the one who left before it all began.

I play them nightly on the ceiling,
these bright dividing selves, this crowd of me,
and think: if there are enough of us,
the difficulty cannot find the real one.

But morning comes and gathers them back,
the sleeper, the writer, the girl at the wrong window,
the flickering ghosts unspooled across the dark—
all of them me, and only me to hold them,

one body walking out to meet the day
carrying its houses, dreams, and unsent mail,
its whole projected legion folded small,
learning at last there was never anywhere to hide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
